First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation: [MATH: \eqalign{ x & =\sqrt x \[3pt] x-\sqrt x & = 0 \[3pt] \sqrt x \left(\sqrt x - 1\right) &= 0 \[3pt] x& = 0, 1 }]

Hence, our limits of integration are from [MATH: x=0] to [MATH: x=1.]

Now, let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

The vertical arrow

  • enters the region through the inner curve [MATH: y=\sqrt{x},] and

  • leaves though the outer curver [MATH: y=x.]

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

  • Step I. Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve [MATH: y=x.]

The corresponding volume is given by [MATH: V_{outer}|= π∫_{0}^{1}[(upper) − (lower)]^{2}dx; = π∫_{0}^{1}[(1) − (x)]^{2}dx; = π∫_{0}^{1}[1 − x]^{2}dx.]

    The corresponding volume is given by [MATH: V_{inner}|= π∫_{0}^{1}[(upper) − (lower)]^{2}dx; = π∫_{0}^{1}[(1) − (sqrt(x))]^{2}dx; = π∫_{0}^{1}[1 − sqrt(x)]^{2}dx.]

    Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as [MATH: \eqalign{ V &= {\color{blue}V_{\text{outer}}} - {\color{red}V_{\text{inner}}} \[5pt] & = \pi \int_0^1 [1-x]^2 - \pi \int_0^1 [1-\sqrt x]^2\,\textrm d x \[5pt] & = \pi \int_0^1 \left((1-x)^2 - (1-\sqrt x)^2\right) \,\textrm d x \[5pt] & = \pi \int_0^1 (x^2-3x+2\sqrt x) \,\,\textrm d x \[5pt] & = \pi\left. \left( \dfrac {1} 3 x^3 - \dfrac{3}{2} x^2 + \dfrac{4}{3} x^{3/2 } \ \right)\right|_0^1\[5pt] & = \pi \left[\left( \dfrac {1}3 (1)^3 - \dfrac{3}{2}(1)^2 + \dfrac{4 }{3}(1)^{3/2 } \right) - (0) \right]\[5pt] & = \pi \left(\dfrac{1}3 - \dfrac{3}{2} +\dfrac{4}{3} \right)\[5pt] & = \dfrac {\pi}{6} . }]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The region enclosed by the curves [MATH: y=x^4] and [MATH: y=x] is shown below. Suppose that this region is rotated [MATH: 2\pi] radians about the horizontal line [MATH: y=-1,] generating a solid of revolution. How can we write an integral expression that gives the volume of the solid?

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/31197dd523b62157c140539a6c7bb69a]

Content:
First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation:

Content:
[MATH: x^{4}|= x; x^{4} − x|= 0; x(x^{3} − 1)|= 0; x|= 0, 1]
Hence, our limits of integration are from [MATH: x=0] to [MATH: x=1.]

Content:
Now, let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d19fa225d96305c254c7fda3d1928585]

Content:
The vertical arrow

Content:
- enters the region through the inner curve [MATH: y=x^4,] and
- leaves though the outer curve [MATH: y=x.]

Content:
Now, we can express the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves, as follows:

Content:
- Step I. Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve [MATH: y=x.]

[IMG: /graphics/d1cee24f623c577a2d488ff8bd022294]

Content:
The corresponding volume is given by
[MATH: V_{outer}|= π∫_{0}^{1}[(upper) − (lower)]^{2}dx; = π∫_{0}^{1}[(x) − (− 1)]^{2}dx; = π∫_{0}^{1}[x + 1]^{2}dx.]

Content:
- Step II. Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve [MATH: y=x^4.]

[IMG: /graphics/21c7edba167c8a95ae98dcb97788e78f]

Content:
The corresponding volume is given by
[MATH: V_{inner}|= π∫_{0}^{1}[(upper) − (lower)]^{2}dx; = π∫_{0}^{1}[(x^{4}) − (− 1)]^{2}dx; = π∫_{0}^{1}[x^{4} + 1]^{2}dx.]

Content:
- Step III. Find the difference.
Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as
[MATH: V|= V_{outer} − V_{inner}; = π∫_{0}^{1}[x + 1]^{2}dx − π∫_{0}^{1}[x^{4} + 1]^{2}dx; = π∫_{0}^{1}([x + 1]^{2} − [x^{4} + 1]^{2})dx.]

[IMG: /graphics/26d52e22b6284d5f166889cd0f35f3ba]

The vertical arrow

- enters the region through the inner curve [MATH: y=-2x,] and
- leaves though the outer curver [MATH: y=2x^2.]

Now, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- Step I. Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve [MATH: y=2x^2.]

[IMG: /graphics/f9f05120045a6cb1ab54a5d1f513735c]

The corresponding volume is given by
[MATH: V_{outer}|= π∫_{− 1}^{0}[(upper) − (lower)]^{2}dx; = π∫_{− 1}^{0}[(3) − (2x^{2})]^{2}dx; = π∫_{− 1}^{0}[3 − 2x^{2}]^{2}dx.]

- Step II. Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve [MATH: y=-2x.]

[IMG: /graphics/c397de2c500adcfa747a095cbd9033a8]

[MATH: V_{inner}|= π∫_{− 1}^{0}[(upper) − (lower)]^{2}dx; = π∫_{− 1}^{0}[(3) − (− 2x)]^{2}dx; = π∫_{− 1}^{0}[3 + 2x]^{2}dx.]

- Step III. Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as
[MATH: V|= V_{outer} − V_{inner}; = π∫_{− 1}^{0}[3 − 2x^{2}]^{2}dx − π∫_{− 1}^{0}[3 + 2x]^{2}dx; = π∫_{− 1}^{0}([3 − 2x^{2}]^{2} − [3 + 2x]^{2})dx.]

Item 5 — Example: Computing the Volume of a Solid Generated by Rotation About a Horizontal Line

Example Prompt:
The region below enclosed by the curves [MATH: y=\sqrt x] and [MATH: y=x] is rotated [MATH: 2\pi] radians about the line [MATH: y=1.] Find the volume of the resulting solid.

[IMG: /graphics/fd2a465e5383ce2e54d3ee87f7eb4128]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation:
[MATH: \eqalign{
x & =\sqrt x \[3pt]
x-\sqrt x & = 0 \[3pt]
\sqrt x \left(\sqrt x - 1\right) &= 0 \[3pt]
x& = 0, 1
}]

Hence, our limits of integration are from [MATH: x=0] to [MATH: x=1.]

Now, let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

[IMG: /graphics/216e98318140f5524c172e89271e836a]

The vertical arrow

- enters the region through the inner curve [MATH: y=\sqrt{x},] and
- leaves though the outer curver [MATH: y=x.]

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- Step I. Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve [MATH: y=x.]

[IMG: /graphics/e2d2e4b6607e0f4e076535b6ff651b03]

The corresponding volume is given by
[MATH: V_{outer}|= π∫_{0}^{1}[(upper) − (lower)]^{2}dx; = π∫_{0}^{1}[(1) − (x)]^{2}dx; = π∫_{0}^{1}[1 − x]^{2}dx.]

- Step II. Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve [MATH: y=\sqrt{x}.]

[IMG: /graphics/ae9f20b7511c5ffe0d37ae0e1e41b9e2]

The corresponding volume is given by
[MATH: V_{inner}|= π∫_{0}^{1}[(upper) − (lower)]^{2}dx; = π∫_{0}^{1}[(1) − (sqrt(x))]^{2}dx; = π∫_{0}^{1}[1 − sqrt(x)]^{2}dx.]
- Step III. Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as
[MATH: \eqalign{
V &= {\color{blue}V_{\text{outer}}} - {\color{red}V_{\text{inner}}} \[5pt]
& = \pi \int_0^1 [1-x]^2 - \pi \int_0^1 [1-\sqrt x]^2\,\textrm d x \[5pt]
& = \pi \int_0^1 \left((1-x)^2 - (1-\sqrt x)^2\right) \,\textrm d x \[5pt]
& = \pi \int_0^1 (x^2-3x+2\sqrt x) \,\,\textrm d x \[5pt]
& = \pi\left. \left( \dfrac {1} 3 x^3 - \dfrac{3}{2} x^2 + \dfrac{4}{3} x^{3/2 } \ \right)\right|_0^1\[5pt]
& = \pi \left[\left( \dfrac {1}3 (1)^3 - \dfrac{3}{2}(1)^2 + \dfrac{4 }{3}(1)^{3/2 } \right) - (0) \right]\[5pt]
& = \pi \left(\dfrac{1}3 - \dfrac{3}{2} +\dfrac{4}{3} \right)\[5pt]
& = \dfrac {\pi}{6} .
}]

- leaves though the outer curve [MATH: x={2-y^2}.]

- Step I. Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve [MATH: x={2-y^2}.]

[IMG: /graphics/e316b962c107bdc757117251c126cedf]

The corresponding volume is given by
[MATH: V_{outer}|= π∫_{− 1}^{1}[(right) − (left)]^{2}dy; = π∫_{− 1}^{1}[(2 − y^{2}) − (− 1)]^{2}dy; = π∫_{− 1}^{1}[3 − y^{2}]^{2}dy.]
- Step II. Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve [MATH: x=y^2.]

[IMG: /graphics/95f6918d6ec3592d8a6e05998dc28886]
